builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA
summary: The method replaces standard federated LoRA, in which clients train and transmit both A and B, with a frozen, periodically resampled random A so only B is trained and uploaded, plus learning rates scaled to each client's adaptation rank. It cuts client compute and uplink traffic roughly in half, but requires rank-dependent learning-rate scheduling, coordination of A resampling across rounds, and adds a stochastic projection whose gradient noise grows at low ranks. It can fail when many clients must use very low ranks, when rank heterogeneity makes the rank-scaled learning rates unstable, or when the convergence assumptions do not match non-IID production data; it also presumes a federated setting that single-GPU practitioners may not have.
rationale: The technique is promising for cost-constrained federated fine-tuning, but its benefits are demonstrated only in a federated setup the reader likely does not operate and depend on rank heterogeneity and convergence assumptions that need validation beyond the paper's benchmarks.
technique: Frozen-A LoRA with rank-aware client learning rates

claims.statement: The method replaces standard federated LoRA, in which clients train and transmit both A and B, with a frozen, periodically resampled random A so only B is trained and uploaded, plus learning rates scaled to each client's adaptation rank. It cuts client compute and uplink traffic roughly in half, but requires rank-dependent learning-rate scheduling, coordination of A resampling across rounds, and adds a stochastic projection whose gradient noise grows at low ranks. It can fail when many clients must use very low ranks, when rank heterogeneity makes the rank-scaled learning rates unstable, or when the convergence assumptions do not match non-IID production data; it also presumes a federated setting that single-GPU practitioners may not have.

The paper reports a 50% reduction in client computational and uplink communication overhead by freezing and periodically resampling A, and claims SPRA-LoRA outperforms federated LoRA baselines at half the client overhead.
